IBS: a common gut disorder you can manage

Irritable bowel syndrome is a long-term gut condition that does not damage the bowel. Learn what it is, what helps, and when to see a doctor.

The basics

What is IBS?

IBS is a functional gut disorder. The bowel looks healthy on scans and tests, but the way it moves and senses is disrupted. The result is recurring belly pain, bloating and a changed bowel habit.

IBS does not damage the intestine and does not increase the risk of bowel cancer.

Pick a pattern to see how doctors describe it. Patterns can shift over time.

The drivers

Why does it happen?

There is no single cause. Research points to several factors working together:

  • Gut-brain axis: the brain and gut miscommunicate, so stress and emotions can trigger symptoms.
  • Sensitive gut nerves: normal gas or stool is felt as pain or urgency.
  • Gut microbes: bacteria can differ in people with IBS, and symptoms sometimes begin after a severe gut infection.
  • Food intolerances: lactose and fermentable sugars (FODMAPs) are common triggers.
  • Hormones: IBS is diagnosed more often in women.

Illustration is artwork for education, not a medical diagram.

What it feels like

Common symptoms

  • Belly pain or cramps, often linked to passing stool
  • Bloating and excess gas
  • Diarrhea, constipation, or switching between both
  • Feeling that the bowel has not fully emptied
  • Urgency, especially when diarrhea is the main problem

Symptoms usually come and go over months and years.

Day to day

Managing IBS without medication

Pictures are illustrations, not photos of real patients.

  1. Eat regularly. Do not skip meals or leave long gaps, and take time over food.
  2. Drink enough. About 8 cups of fluid a day, mostly water or non-caffeinated drinks. Keep tea and coffee to 3 cups and go easy on alcohol and fizzy drinks.
  3. Watch the classic triggers. Fatty and spicy meals, caffeine, and sugar-free sweeteners such as sorbitol.
  4. Try a short low-FODMAP trial. 2 to 6 weeks, then reintroduce foods one at a time, ideally with a pharmacist or dietitian.
  5. Choose fiber wisely. Favor soluble fiber (oats, psyllium). Large amounts of bran can worsen bloating.
  6. Move more. Regular activity, even walking, helps symptoms and stress.
  7. Manage stress. Relaxation, deep breathing and yoga. Gut-directed therapy such as CBT or hypnotherapy can help when symptoms persist.

What about probiotics?

The evidence is mixed. If you try one, take it at the recommended dose for at least 4 weeks and judge by your own symptoms.

Treatment

Medicines: chosen by your main symptom

There is no single IBS pill. Medicines relieve symptoms rather than cure them, and the choice follows your main problem.

  • Crampy pain: antispasmodics such as dicyclomine or hyoscine, taken as needed
  • Constipation: a soluble fiber supplement such as psyllium (ispaghula); laxatives if needed
  • Diarrhea: loperamide is the usual first choice

Let a professional choose

The right medicine and dose depend on your main symptom and your history. Ask a doctor or pharmacist rather than self-medicating long term.

Safety

When to see a doctor

See a doctor promptly if you have

  • Unexplained weight loss
  • Blood in the stool or rectal bleeding
  • Diarrhea that wakes you at night
  • Unexplained vomiting
  • Iron-deficiency anemia
  • Pain not relieved by passing gas or stool
  • A persistent change in your bowel habits

These can point to something more serious and need proper checking. IBS is a diagnosis a professional makes, so do not self-diagnose.
